title: Episode 5 (lines 924–1053)

teacherSummary.text: The blind prophet Teiresias warns Creon that the birds and altars show the gods' anger: the unburied body pollutes the city. He urges Creon to yield. Creon insults him as a money-getter. Teiresias prophesies that Creon will pay with a child of his own. Shaken, Creon decides to bury Polyneices and free Antigone.

context.history: Teiresias, the same seer as in Oedipus Rex, brings the gods' judgment. Signs from birds and sacrifices were standard means of divination.

significance: Creon finally bends, but too late. The play's lesson, "To err is common," is offered and almost accepted.

items.prompt: Analyze how Teiresias' speech moves from evidence to counsel to warning.
items.expected: Teiresias first reports evidence: sitting at his “throne of augury,” he hears birds in “twitterings, hoots, and screams” tearing one another, then finds the sacrifice by fire fail, a “foul ooze” from the thigh bones and altars that will not kindle (lines 938–953). He interprets the signs as Creon’s “wilful temper” profaning the shrines with the unburied son, and he offers counsel: “To err is common,” but the man who “repents and seeks / The cure” is not unwise; “Let death disarm thy vengeance” (lines 954–970). Only after Creon insults him as a profit-seeker does he warn that Creon shall pay “life for life,” a living soul entombed and a corpse left “unlaved, unwept, unsepulchred” (lines 1003–1010). The structure shows a seer who tries reason before revelation.

items.prompt: How does the episode develop the theme of seeing and blindness?
items.expected: Teiresias is blind and needs a boy to guide him, yet he reads the signs of the gods and sees what Creon cannot. Creon, who can see, is blind to his own error and calls the seer a fraud. The contrast shows that true sight is insight, and that the powerful king is the one truly in the dark.

anchorPassages.note: Polluted rites: the unburied corpse makes heaven refuse the city's offerings.
anchorPassages.text:
The divination of my arts shall tell.
Sitting upon my throne of augury,
As is my wont, where every fowl of heaven
Finds harbourage, upon mine ears was borne
A jargon strange of twitterings, hoots, and screams,
So knew I that each bird at the other tare
With bloody talons, for the whirr of wings
Could signify nought else. Perturbed in soul,
I straight essayed the sacrifice by fire
On blazing altars, but the God of Fire
Came not in flame, and from the thigh bones dripped
And sputtered in the ashes a foul ooze;
Gall-bladders cracked and spurted up: the fat
Melted and fell and left the thigh bones bare.
Such are the signs, taught by this lad, I read—
As I guide others, so the boy guides me—
The frustrate signs of oracles grown dumb.

locator.opening: The divination of my arts shall tell.
locator.closing: The frustrate signs of oracles grown dumb.
locator.landmark: Teiresias: birds tear each other; sacrifice fails; oracles grown dumb

anchorPassages.note: Counsel of repentance: death should disarm vengeance; obstinacy is the true folly.
anchorPassages.text:
O King, thy wilful temper ails the State,
For all our shrines and altars are profaned
By what has filled the maw of dogs and crows,
The flesh of Oedipus’ unburied son.
Therefore the angry gods abominate
Our litanies and our burnt offerings;
Therefore no birds trill out a happy note,
Gorged with the carnival of human gore.
O ponder this, my son. To err is common
To all men, but the man who having erred
Hugs not his errors, but repents and seeks
The cure, is not a wastrel nor unwise.
No fool, the saw goes, like the obstinate fool.
Let death disarm thy vengeance. O forbear
To vex the dead. What glory wilt thou win
By slaying twice the slain? I mean thee well;
Counsel’s most welcome if it promise gain.

locator.closing: Counsel’s most welcome if it promise gain.
locator.landmark: Teiresias: thy wilful temper ails the State; err, then repent; do not vex the dead twice

anchorPassages.note: Doom spelled out: Creon's inverted burials will be paid with his own child's life.
anchorPassages.text:
Know then for sure, the coursers of the sun
Not many times shall run their race, before
Thou shalt have given the fruit of thine own loins
In quittance of thy murder, life for life;
For that thou hast entombed a living soul,
And sent below a denizen of earth,
And wronged the nether gods by leaving here
A corpse unlaved, unwept, unsepulchred.
Herein thou hast no part, nor e’en the gods
In heaven; and thou usurp’st a power not thine.
For this the avenging spirits of Heaven and Hell
Who dog the steps of sin are on thy trail:
What these have suffered thou shalt suffer too.
And now, consider whether bought by gold
I prophesy. For, yet a little while,
And sound of lamentation shall be heard,
Of men and women through thy desolate halls;
And all thy neighbour States are leagued to avenge
Their mangled warriors who have found a grave
I’ the maw of wolf or hound, or wingèd bird
That flying homewards taints their city’s air.
These are the shafts, that like a bowman I,
Provoked to anger, loosen at thy breast,
Unerring, and their smart thou shalt not shun.

locator.closing: Unerring, and their smart thou shalt not shun.

anchorPassages.text:
My liege, the man hath gone, foretelling woe.
And, O believe me, since these grizzled locks
Were like the raven, never have I known
The prophet’s warning to the State to fail.
I know it too, and it perplexes me.
To yield is grievous, but the obstinate soul
That fights with Fate, is smitten grievously.
Son of Menoeceus, list to good advice.

anchorPassages.note: Reversal too late in timing still decisive in will. Resumes after pending line 1038.
anchorPassages.text:
Go, free the maiden from her rocky cell;
And for the unburied outlaw build a tomb.
Is that your counsel? You would have me yield?
Yea, king, this instant. Vengeance of the gods
Is swift to overtake the impenitent.
Ah! what a wrench it is to sacrifice
My heart’s resolve; but Fate is ill to fight.
Go, trust not others. Do it quick thyself.
I go hot-foot. Bestir ye one and all,
My henchmen! Get ye axes! Speed away
To yonder eminence! I too will go,
For all my resolution this way sways.
’Twas I that bound, I too will set her free.
Almost I am persuaded it is best
To keep through life the law ordained of old. Exit Creon.

segments.script: Teiresias, the same seer as in Oedipus Rex, brings the gods' judgment. Signs from birds and sacrifices were standard means of divination. Creon finally bends, but too late. The play's lesson, "To err is common," is offered and almost accepted. Conflict: Teiresias brings the gods’ anger into the open: polluted altars against Creon’s insults; prophecy against a king who calls all prophets a “money-getting tribe.” Foreshadowing: The threat that Creon will pay with a child of his own points straight at Haemon before the Messenger confirms it. Characterization: Creon moves from scorn to the admission that “To yield is grievous,” the first crack in the stubbornness that has defined him. Watch for burial and the unburied body: Bird-signs and choked altars make the corpse a civic pollution; Creon’s late decision to bury Polyneices and free Antigone tries to undo both wrongs at once.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “O ponder this, my son. To err is common / To all men, but the man who having erred / Hugs not his errors, but repents and seeks / The cure, is not a wastrel nor unwise” slowly and put it in my own words: Teiresias tells Creon that everyone errs, but a man who does not hug his error and who seeks a cure is neither a wastrel nor unwise. Next, craft. “Hugs not his errors” makes stubbornness tactile, as if the mistake were something a person can cling to, and “seeks / The cure” offers a way back before the warning hardens. The strongest word is “repents”: it names the turn still offered before the warning hardens. Then, effect. What do lines 962–965 reveal about the prophet Teiresias? My answer: The prophet Teiresias still offers counsel before he offers doom. “To err is common” is the play’s lesson held out in time for Creon to take it; whether he will is the test of this scene.

To err is common / To all men, but the man who having erred / Hugs not his errors, but repents and seeks / The cure, is not a wastrel nor unwise” (Episode 5, lines 962–965): Teiresias, lines 962–965. On conflict: Teiresias brings the gods’ anger into the open: polluted altars against Creon’s insults; prophecy against a king who calls all prophets a “money-getting tribe.” Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.
